analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally import lower-priced prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to let Americans import cheaper prescription drugs, with 31 cosponsors, sat on the Senate calendar and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end the current ban on bringing prescription drugs back into the United States from countries where they sell for less. Americans could buy FDA-approved medicines from registered pharmacies and exporters in Canada, Australia, most of Europe, Japan, New Zealand, and Switzerland, either through a registered U.S. importer or directly for personal use, limited to a 90-day supply. It backs this with a safety system — registered and inspected importers and exporters, verified chains of custody, tamper-evident shipment markings, recall coordination, and a ban on dealing with unregistered foreign internet pharmacies — and it prohibits drug companies from discriminating against importers or deliberately making their U.S. and foreign products different to defeat importation.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions — especially seniors and anyone on long-term medication — would gain access to the same FDA-approved drugs at prices closer to what consumers in Canada, Europe, and other developed countries pay; the bill's own findings note CBO found such drugs cost 35–55% less abroad [S3]. Registered U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers would gain a new import business.

how_it_helps.text: It waives the current ban on importing U.S.-exported drugs, letting registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals buy the same FDA-approved medicines from Canada, Australia, the EU, Japan, New Zealand, and Switzerland [S2, S3].

It bans drug companies from discriminating against importers — refusing supply, delaying shipments, or engineering differences between the U.S. version and the foreign version of the same drug — and makes foreign resale of properly sold drugs non-infringing [S3].

It imposes real safety controls: registered importers and exporters, facility inspections at least 12 times a year, verified chain of custody, tamper-evident markings, recalls, and limits on personal importation (90-day supply, valid prescription) [S2].
It cracks down on unregistered foreign internet pharmacies by blocking their transactions from U.S. payment systems, steering consumers to vetted sellers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose U.S. price premiums and control over distribution would be eroded by competition from their own products sold abroad; they would also bear compliance costs from the anti-discrimination and product-uniformity rules [S3].

drawbacks.text: Imported drugs could differ from U.S. versions in inactive ingredients or fail bioequivalence, so the bill required allergy warnings and possible non-bioequivalence advisories — meaning some patients could receive a variant of their drug that is not identical to the U.S. version [S3].

The safety machinery — registration, inspections, track-and-trace, 90-day personal-supply limits, exclusion of biologics and injectables — is complex and would impose compliance costs and new fees on importers and exporters, costs that could partly show up in prices [S2, S3].

Drug manufacturers argued then, and critics generally argue, that price arbitrage from markets where drugs are sold more cheaply could reduce revenues that fund research and development of new medicines — a cost an honest supporter must weigh, even though the bill's findings note Americans currently pay the highest brand-name prices in the world [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—cheaper medicine for tens of millions of Americans—is large, and the bill took the safety objection seriously: it built registration, inspection, chain-of-custody, labeling, recall, and personal-import limits rather than opening the border to anything. The costs are real but modest: it would pressure manufacturers' U.S. revenues (some of which fund research into drugs that may not pay off), and new import oversight would be an administrative burden. On balance, the main reason it died was not its design but the industry it would take revenue from.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 31 cosponsors, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar in June 2009 — but no committee or floor vote ever happened, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2011 [S5, S1].

narrative.text: Dorgan introduced the bill on June 10, 2009 with 31 cosponsors spanning both parties, including Republican senators Snowe, Grassley, McCain, Collins, Thune, and Vitter [S4, S3].

The only Senate actions were introduction, two readings, and placement on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 73) on June 11, 2009; no committee reported it and no vote was ever scheduled [S5].
The bill remained on the calendar until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, at which point it died without a floor vote [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, whose U.S. pricing power and control over supply went unchallenged; American consumers kept paying among the world's highest brand-name drug prices [S3].

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — 24 of 58 Democrats, 6 of 40 Republicans, and the Senate's lone Independent cosponsored — but the bill never received a vote in either chamber, so no roll-call split exists [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill directly attacks the price gap they maintain between the U.S. and other wealthy countries: it allows reimportation, bans supply manipulation and price discrimination against importers, and outlaws manufacturing differences designed to defeat importation [S2, S3]. Their core U.S. pricing power is the bill's target.
Registered pharmacies and wholesalers can become importers of cheaper foreign-supplied drugs, a new line of business, though they bear registration fees, inspections, and recordkeeping [S3].
Registered exporters gain a large legal market of American customers; unregistered internet pharmacies lose, since their transactions are barred from U.S. payment systems [S2, S3].
The bill makes processing payments for unregistered foreign pharmacies a prohibited act, shrinking gray-market online drug sales while legitimizing registered ones [S2].
